1:
Chrysostom notices something odd about where this subject stands. Having finished with doctrine and turning to what belongs to conduct, Paul dismisses everything else and goes straight to the chief of good things, almsgiving, and having treated that alone he leaves off; elsewhere he closes his letters with temperance and meekness and long-suffering and the rest. Chrysostom's answer is that the greater part of what came before was already ethical — the fornicator chastised, those going to law before Gentiles corrected, the drunkards and gluttons terrified, the seditious and contentious condemned, the unworthy communicants delivered over to that intolerable sentence, love itself expounded — so that only the one pressing matter was left, the aid required for the saints. Gill identifies them as the poor believers at Jerusalem, reduced to want either by the spoiling of their goods at the hands of their persecuting countrymen or by the selling of their possessions into a common stock now exhausted, partly by living on it and partly by spending it to spread the gospel among the Gentiles. Wesley will spare only a line, but it is the sharpest in the chapter: the saints is a more solemn and a more affecting word than if he had said the poor. Ellicott makes that the hinge — the apostle does not call them the poor but the saints, and that was the true ground of their claim upon their brethren.

Ellicott reads the need itself as evidence: the very necessity of a collection shows that the community of goods established at the beginning in Jerusalem had not proved successful, since Christianity was largely recruited from the lower classes and a common fund could not long flourish with so few contributors and so great a multitude of sharers; and many shut up in prison had perhaps by now been released in abject poverty. Calvin traces the occasion further back, to the famine Agabus foretold under Claudius, and grounds the duty in gratitude: the Gentile churches were bound, if they would not be held guilty of very great ingratitude, to relieve the place from which they had received the gospel. Barnes hears the definite article as proof that the matter was already familiar — not news to them, so that every instruction here concerns the manner of giving and not the occasion or the duty. He presses that distinction hard: the word rendered order does not mean Paul assumed authority to tax them, and the collection was cheerful and voluntary in all the churches.

On the word itself the bench has been overtaken by evidence. Barnes reports that the term for collection occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and is not found in the classical writers, deriving it from the ordinary verb to gather. Robertson can now correct him: it comes from a late verb meaning to collect, recently turned up in the papyri and inscriptions, and the noun is chiefly found in documents recording religious collections for a god or a temple. Robertson adds that the introduction of the topic may seem sudden, but the Corinthians were simply behind with their part and may even have asked about it — they had promised long before, and now must do what they pledged. Henry watches the tact of it: this was no peculiar service demanded of them, only the same rule already given to Galatia, and Paul names those churches to stir emulation, since a congregation excelling most others in gifts and probably in wealth would not suffer itself to come behind any in bounty. Ellicott adds that the order was given in Galatia in person rather than by letter, and quotes Bengel's summary of the method — the Galatians proposed to the Corinthians, the Corinthians to the Macedonians, both to the Romans, for great is the power of examples.
2:
The phrase behind upon the first day of the week is literally on one of the sabbaths, and the bench agrees on what that means without agreeing on what follows from it. Barnes notes that the Jews used sabbath for the seven-day period itself, so that it is universally agreed the first day is meant. Robertson adds the grammar: the cardinal one stands for the ordinal first after the Hebrew fashion familiar from the Greek Old Testament. Ellicott calls it a Hebrew idiom equivalent to the day next after the sabbath, and observes that the day of the resurrection had already become the natural one for Christian work and worship though not yet by the title Christendom later used — that name appears first in John's vision on Patmos, and the practice of assembling then is visible at Troas. Gill guards against reading too much into the plural: an ancient copy of Beza's adds the Lord's day, and the Syriac and Arabic render it every first day, but the apostle intends some one first day, not a standing weekly ordinance — for the reason he gives is that there be no gatherings when he comes, and a permanent rule would have run on through his visit as well as before it.

Clarke draws the firmest conclusion from the day, reading it as a strong argument for keeping the Christian sabbath, since the first day was evidently when the principal meetings were held at Corinth and in Galatia and therefore wherever Christianity had spread. He also finds the practice's shape in the synagogue: the Jews regularly collected for the poor on the sabbath so that the needy should not be kept from coming, and they kept a purse of alms, what we would call the poor's box — which Clarke takes to be exactly what lay by him in store refers to. Calvin will not go so far, and twice declines Chrysostom's readings. He thinks the probability is that the apostles at first retained the day already in use and only later, pressed by superstition, set it aside for another, the resurrection day being chosen because it ended the shadows of the law, so that the day itself reminds us of Christian liberty. He grants that believers have always had a fixed day of rest, because assemblies cannot be held daily; and he reads the apostle's warning elsewhere against distinguishing days as aimed at religion, not at external order.

Where the money was to rest is genuinely disputed. Robertson takes the phrase plainly — by himself, in his home, treasuring it up, with the present imperative making it a habit. Barnes reads it the same way, laying stress on the privacy: let a man set apart a portion at home, calmly, not under the influence of pathetic appeals nor for the sake of display among others but as a matter of principle. Yet Barnes then allows that the closing clause seems to demand a common treasury after all, and Ellicott rejects the domestic reading outright — he cannot think with Stanley that each was to store it in his own house, since the stated object is that the sum be ready in bulk when the apostle arrives, which would fail if the offering still had to be gathered from every Christian home. On the measure all agree it is proportional and universal. Ellicott renders it whatsoever he may be prospered in, and denies that only exceptional prosperity obliges a man. Wesley presses it further: not the rich only, but let him that hath little gladly give of that little, increasing his alms as God increases his substance; a tenth is merely the lowest rule of Christian prudence, and he shows a more excellent way — stint yourself to no proportion at all, but lend to God all you can.
3:
A comma decides this verse, and the bench is split over where to put it. Barnes lays out both camps. Macknight and Doddridge take the letters to be neither to nor from the apostle but letters signed and sent by the Corinthian church itself, designating its messengers and certifying their authority — the reading the usual pointing of the Greek supports, and the one our version follows. Against them Griesbach, Locke, Rosenmuller, Bloomfield, Beza, Hammond, Grotius and Whitby put the comma after approve, so that the sense runs: whom you designate, them I will send with letters to carry your charity to Jerusalem. Mill doubted whether that construction accords with Greek usage, but Barnes thinks the weight of those names settles the point and that the second reading better fits the passage's design. Clarke arrives by another road at the same place. He asks the obvious question — why should Paul want letters of approbation for men he would shortly meet face to face, and could examine himself? — and suggests either that the reference is to letters of recommendation the Corinthians had already sent him while he was away, or that Bishop Pearce is right to render it ye shall have approved, in which case the difficulty vanishes. Clarke's own verdict on the alternative punctuation is that it seems most natural.

Robertson supplies what the letters were for: they made the appointment formal and regular, and he notes that the verb behind approve means to test and so to approve. Ellicott reads the whole verse as a man still deciding. The apostle had not settled whether he would carry the gift himself or accredit messengers with letters, and would be governed by how much was collected and how urgent the need at Jerusalem proved to be. Then Ellicott adds a remark of unusual psychological candour: Paul was in one sense the humblest of men, but he valued the dignity of his apostolic office highly, and had only a very small sum been ready he would have felt it beneath that office — though not beneath himself — to be its bearer. Barnes reaches the same conclusion from the next verse, which shows Paul willing to go but not expecting to; and if he did not go, nothing was more natural than to offer letters commending the men sent to the favour and hospitality of the church in Judea. Gill glosses the opening clause simply, that the coming meant is to Corinth, and very quickly.

Calvin states the principle the arrangement serves. We give cheerfully when we know for certain that what we give is well laid out; so the apostle points the Corinthians to a method by which they may be assured of a good and faithful administration, namely the selecting of approved persons to whom the matter may be entrusted. That he then offers his own services, if they wish it, Calvin takes as evidence that he has the business at heart. On the word rendered liberality, Barnes observes that it is the ordinary word for grace or favour, used here of an act of grace — a kindness, a benefaction conferred; Ellicott simply renders it gifts. Robertson closes the account from history: the messengers of the churches did in the end travel with Paul to Jerusalem, though he notes as a curiosity that no name from Corinth appears in the list of companions Luke records.
4:
The condition is about the size of the gift, not the convenience of the apostle. Gill glosses it as meaning that if it should be convenient, or thought proper and expedient, that he go — and he notes the ancient versions sharpen this, the Syriac reading if this work should be worthy that I should go and the Arabic if the thing should be worthy to go with me. That is, if so large a collection be made that it is worthy of an apostle's escort; by which, Gill observes drily, he is artfully pressing them toward a good collection. Robertson confirms the sense from the grammar, rendering it if the collection be worthy of the going as to me also, and remarking that once the construction is seen the awkward phrase clears up. Barnes puts the same thought in practical terms: if his presence would further the object, or satisfy the Corinthians better, or be needed to guide and aid the men they sent, he was willing to go with them.

Both Barnes and Clarke break off here to commend Paley's account of how the apostle handled money, Barnes noting that the question at issue is management so delicate as never to excite suspicion and so to preserve a blameless reputation. Clarke quotes the argument at length. First, Paley observes, Paul disclaims any inspired authority for the directions he is giving — he speaks not by commandment, but on occasion of the forwardness of others and to prove the sincerity of their love. Who, Paley asks, that had a sinister purpose to serve by recommending subscriptions would thus draw the distinction, and thus lower the credit of his own recommendation? Second, though he asserts the general right of Christian ministers to a maintenance from their ministry, and grants that the Lord has ordained that they who preach the gospel should live of the gospel, he protests against using that right himself: he has used none of these things, nor written that it should be so done to him, since it were better for him to die than that any man should make his glorying — that is, his professions of disinterestedness — void.

Paley's third observation is the one this verse supplies. Repeatedly the apostle proposes that there be associates with him in the management of the public bounty, and pointedly not colleagues of his own appointment but persons elected for the purpose by the contributors themselves; whomsoever they approve, them he will send, and if he goes too they shall go with him. What is here only proposed, Clarke adds, we find in the second epistle actually done, and done for the very purpose of guarding his character against any imputation that might arise in the discharge of a trust involving money — the brother sent with Titus being one whose praise in the gospel ran through all the churches, and who was moreover chosen by the churches themselves to travel with the gift. Wesley compresses the whole of it into five words on the closing clause: they shall go with me, to remove any possible suspicion.
5:
Gill hears the promise as a rebuttal: Paul assures them again that he really does intend to come, because some had given out that he would never come to them any more and hoped they should never see him again. Barnes fills in what lay behind that rumour. Paul had originally expected to see Corinth on the way to Macedonia and had for some reason abandoned that particular design — but not the visit itself, only its order, so that he now means to work through the Macedonian churches first and reach Corinth afterwards. Clarke explains why this counts as a detour worth mentioning: Macedonia was not on the direct road from Ephesus to Corinth at all, lying at the upper end of the Aegean and very far out of his line, and it is precisely because of that that Paul says he does pass through it — the journey is deliberate, not incidental. Robertson makes the same point from the tense, the present indicative here being the futuristic use, so that the sense is simply I plan to pass through; Wesley's whole comment is that he purposes going that way.

The clause has also carried a long argument about where the letter was written. Ellicott is blunt that a misrepresentation of these words gave rise to the incorrect note at the end of the chapter in our English Bibles which places the writing at Philippi: the apostle is not saying where he is at the moment but what he intends for his journey. Clarke reports that almost all now allow, against that subscription, that the letter came from Ephesus, and thinks the following verses put the question past doubt. Calvin sets out the common opinion fairly before rejecting it — persons travelling from Philippi to Corinth by land did have to cross Macedonia — and then gives three reasons for Ephesus: that Paul says shortly he will remain where he is until Pentecost, that he sends greetings not from the churches of Macedonia but from the churches of Asia, and that in the second epistle he states explicitly that he crossed into Macedonia only after this letter had gone.

Calvin also draws out what the route cost. He could have sailed by a straight course to Achaia; visiting Macedonia required a long circuit and a more disagreeable road, and that he chose it anyway, then promised the Corinthians something further, shows his affection toward them — for what reason had he to delay except that he was concerned for their welfare? Henry reads the plan the same way and turns it into a rule. The heart of a truly Christian minister must be much toward the people among whom he has long laboured with remarkable success; no wonder Paul was willing to stay at Corinth as long as his other duties allowed. Some there despised him and had made a faction against him, yet many loved him tenderly and paid him the respect due to an apostle and their spiritual father, and as for the rest he might hope that a longer stay would reduce them to a better temper and rectify what was out of order. That prospect, Henry says, is itself a just reason for an apostle to make his abode in a place.
6:
The hedging is deliberate. Gill notes that Paul could not be certain what calls in Providence might arise to some other place where his presence would be needed, so the winter is offered as a possibility and not a promise. Robertson finds the same reserve in the words themselves: the phrase rendered it may be is a participle pressed into service as an adverb, found in Plato and Xenophon but nowhere else in the New Testament, and the verb for wintering is a late formation used of putting in for the bad season. Ellicott hears a warmth in the change of plan — the former arrangement had allowed only a brief call at Corinth, whereas this one would permit a longer stay, and it is with affectionate emphasis that Paul then asks to be sent forward on his way. Clarke supplies the whole projected itinerary in a line: Pentecost at Ephesus, then Macedonia and probably the summer there, then Corinth in the autumn and the winter spent with them.

What the sending forward amounted to is read two ways. Clarke and Barnes take it materially. Barnes glosses it as accompanying him, aiding him, furnishing him the means of going, and observes that it was customary for the apostles to travel attended by members of the churches and friends. Clarke is more specific still: in most cases the different churches paid his expenses on to the next, and where a church did not, he worked at his trade to acquire the means of travelling. Ellicott does not deny the provision but refuses to stop there — the phrase implies not merely that Corinth should be the starting point of the journey to Jerusalem, but that he should set out on it with the good wishes and the blessing of his Corinthian friends. Barnes adds that the destination was probably Judea, though wherever Paul went it would have gratified him to have their company.

Neither the destination nor the departure went as written. Ellicott points out that where he would go on from Corinth had not yet been settled, and in the event was settled for him: he did remain three months there through the winter, and when the season made a voyage safe he resolved to sail for Syria, but a conspiracy against him — discovered in time — forced that plan to be abandoned for a different route by way of Troas. Robertson confirms both halves of it from the record, that Paul did stay the three months, probably this very winter, and that he had to flee a plot laid against him. The indefinite clause about wherever he might go, Robertson notes, turns out to have been well chosen.
7:
Gill catches the tone of the refusal exactly. Paul will not see them now by the way — that is, he will not merely look in on them and be gone, like a wayfaring man who turns aside for a single night. Robertson confirms that the Greek phrase carries the same casualness our own idiom does when we say something in passing: it means incidentally, a call made en route to somewhere else. Clarke notes how easy such a call would have been, since from Ephesus to Corinth was merely a crossing of the Aegean and comparatively a short passage; the point is therefore not distance but the kind of visit Paul refuses to pay. Ellicott simply records that this is one more reference to the changed intention, and Wesley reduces the whole clause to a schedule — not, he says, until I have been in Macedonia.

Barnes reads the same clause as evidence of a decision already taken. Something had occurred to change Paul's mind and induce him to reach Macedonia by another way, so that the brief visit on the outward leg is now off; what he hopes for instead is to remain a while with them on the return, and the Greek is modest about even that, saying only that he hopes to stay a little while. The whole plan then rests on a condition, and Barnes thinks the qualification is the important word in the verse. The apostle does not use the language of certainty and confidence. He felt his dependence upon God and regarded everything as under his direction, and Barnes points out that the same reservation appears in an earlier chapter of this letter, so that it is a settled habit of speech rather than a passing scruple.

Robertson describes the grammar of that reservation as a condition of the third class, the form used for what is genuinely open, and draws the same conclusion in five words: Paul did everything in the Lord. The convergence is worth marking, since Barnes reaches it from Paul's psychology and Robertson from his syntax, and the two arrive together. Between them the verse leaves the itinerary genuinely undecided — a change of route already made, a hoped-for stay of unspecified length, and a permission not yet given.
8:
Barnes takes the naming of Ephesus as decisive for a question outside the verse: this passage proves where the letter was written, and it is by incidental indications of just this kind that the epistles are usually placed at all. Calvin had argued the same from the same clause — the probability is that the apostle speaks of the place he is in, not of one he could reach only by a long circuit, since a traveller from Philippi would have had to leave Corinth when already near it and cross the sea to get to Ephesus. On the date, Gill explains that Pentecost was the feast of weeks or of harvest, fifty days from the passover; Robertson concludes that Paul is writing in the spring, before the feast; and Ellicott places it about Easter-time, adding that the plan was formed under pressure — the hostility of enemies at Ephesus was increasing and had to be subdued, while at the same moment a door had been opened wide for the spread of the gospel. To such a man as Paul, Ellicott says, duty to be done and danger to be faced in the doing of it were together sufficient indication of where he ought to be found.

Why an apostle should date his plans by a Jewish festival at all is the live question, and Calvin argues it against Erasmus, who preferred to render the word as a bare interval and did so, in Calvin's judgement, influenced by frivolous conjectures rather than any solid argument. Erasmus objected that there was as yet no Christian Pentecost such as the church later kept, which Calvin grants; and that the Jewish solemnity cannot be meant, since Paul elsewhere annuls and condemns the superstitious observance of days. That second point Calvin refuses. Paul did not wait for the day out of any superstitious regard to it, but because a larger assembly would gather then and he hoped an opportunity of propagating the gospel would be presented. Calvin adds a grammatical reason for taking it as a named day rather than a count of fifty: the definite article will not let the word mean anything else, and to read it as merely specifying an interval would be an excessively poor sense.

Gill arrives independently at Calvin's conclusion and states it as flatly. The feast was abrogated at the death of Christ, and Paul mentions it not as a festival Christians were obliged to regard or did regard, but simply as marking the length of his stay; and when he was elsewhere eager to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, that too was not to keep it but because people would be there from all parts, to whom he would have opportunity of preaching. Calvin makes the same comparison and sharpens it — others presented themselves at the feast to sacrifice according to the ritual of the law, while Paul had another object, that his ministry might be useful in proportion to the size of the crowd. Whether the stay ran its full course is disputed. Clarke thinks it very probable that it did, and that all these journeys were taken exactly as the apostle had projected them; Robertson holds that the uproar raised by Demetrius apparently hurried Paul out of Ephesus before his own date.
9:
Gill canvasses three accounts of what the open door was. Some take it for the sheer populousness of Ephesus; others for the conversion of certain great men in the city, which had made way for the gospel there; but Gill judges it rather to mean the desire that had appeared in many to hear — they flocked to the word, their hearts were opened to attend to it, and great numbers believed. He puts it neatly as two doors at once: a door of utterance in the apostle himself, and a door of entrance in them. Barnes keeps to the plain figure, the word denoting an occasion or opportunity, the means by which access is had, and so an unobstructed facility for doing good; Calvin says the same, that the metaphor is a common one and the Lord had opened a way for the furthering of the gospel, called great because many might be gained. Clarke alone reaches for something more particular, suggesting that the apostle may be alluding to the flinging open of the great doors of the Circus Maximus before the chariot races began — in which case the adversaries that follow are the competitors already in the field.

What the second adjective means divides them. Wesley distributes the two words neatly: the door is great as to the number of hearers, and effectual as to the effects wrought upon them. Calvin takes it the same way, that the Lord blessed his labour and by the power of the Spirit rendered his doctrine powerful. Clarke reports Bishop Pearce reading it in quite another sense — not effectual at all but full of labour, so that the phrase means a great and energetic door which the apostle perceives will require much toil of him. Robertson goes to the evidence. The word is a late one, and the papyri show it in a medical prescription for something tolerably strong, while the related form is used of a mill in working order, of tilled land, and of wrought iron; in the New Testament it describes the word of God as powerful. Paul's meaning, Robertson concludes, is at least that he has a great opportunity for work.

On the adversaries the bench is unanimous, and the unanimity is the point. Barnes observes that such a setting open of a great door is often the very occasion of increased opposition, and that we should not be surprised to find the same now; but Paul treated it as no reason to leave Ephesus and every reason to remain, taking it for evidence that the Spirit was at work, that the enemies of God were alarmed, and that his own presence was needed to strengthen young converts who would be attacked. Wesley says it in a clause — there must always be adversaries where Satan's kingdom shakes. Calvin presses hardest: this holy man sought Christ's glory everywhere and never chose a place for his own convenience or pleasure, but did not merely refrain from shrinking back, presenting himself of his own accord where he saw he must contend most keenly, and knowing that the fiercer the assault the better equipped and the more resolute he had to be. Robertson describes the opponents as lying lined up against him, agrees that Paul names them as a reason for staying, and then admits the difficulty honestly: and yet Paul suddenly leaves, hinting at much of which we should like to know more.
10:
The conditional opening is not doubt about Timothy but about the roads. Gill notes that Paul had already dispatched him and simply could not say whether unforeseen incidents on the way might prevent his arrival — from which, Gill adds, it is plain that this letter was not carried by Timothy, whatever the subscription at its end claims. Clarke reaches the same verdict and calls that subscription very exceptionable, since Timothy had been sent with Erastus from Ephesus into Macedonia. Ellicott explains why the two might cross: Timothy and Erastus were to travel through Macedonia, delaying at the various churches on the way, whereas this letter would go by a more direct route, so that it could easily arrive first. Calvin simply observes that Paul speaks as though not yet certain of the visit. Their errand, on Ellicott's account, was to recall the Corinthians to the apostle's teaching and check the evils rumour had reported.

Why such an errand should need protecting is the burden of the verse. Henry puts it bluntly: Timothy came not only to direct but to blame, to censure and reprove the culpable, and he came into a church wholly in factions where mutual strife and hatred ran very high, where some were rich and many proud on account both of outward wealth and of spiritual gifts — and proud spirits cannot easily bear reproof. It was therefore reasonable to think that young Timothy might be roughly used, and Henry draws the rule that Christians should bear faithful reproofs from their ministers rather than terrify and discourage them from their duty. Barnes adds that Timothy might well feel embarrassed among the rich, the gay and the great, and that the false teachers he would have to withstand were powerful and might try to intimidate him. Ellicott presses further still — Timothy was young in years and young in the faith, probably of a constitutionally weak and timid nature, and officially very subordinate; in a church where some had gone so far as to question the apostle's own authority, that was real danger. Robertson agrees in a sentence that Paul evidently had reason to fear the treatment Timothy might receive.

Chrysostom turns the whole caution around, and his is the most striking reading on the bench. Someone may think the advice unworthy of Timothy's courage, he says; but it is not said on Timothy's account at all — it is said for the hearers' sake, lest by their designs against him they should injure themselves. Timothy for his part had his station always in the way of dangers, having served with Paul in the gospel as a child serves a father. What Paul fears is that from boldness toward the disciple they will proceed to the teacher and grow worse, or that in revenge for the master's rebuke they will exact satisfaction from the messenger; and so he checks them from far off. Chrysostom hears the emphasis fall on the last two words: tell me not of those without, the Gentiles and unbelievers — it is your part I require, you for whom the whole letter was composed. Calvin narrows the danger, denying that Timothy's life was at risk and locating the threat in the many enemies of Christ who would oppose him, and then generalises: the church ought to be concerned for the preservation of its ministers' lives, and the more a man is endowed with gifts for edification and applies himself to it, the dearer his life should be to us. On the closing clause Calvin allows two senses, commendation of Timothy or a plain statement that the two men held one office, both labouring in the word; Wesley takes it as the true ground of reverence to pastors, and concludes that those who work the Lord's work no one ought to despise.
11:
The contempt to be guarded against is contempt for youth, and the bench adds two further shades to it. Barnes expects the trouble from the wealthy and proud who valued themselves on their wisdom and experience, and recalls that Paul elsewhere charged Timothy so to live that no one should have occasion to despise his youth; a young minister, Barnes says, should receive the respect due to his office, and if he conducts himself according to his calling his youth should be no barrier to the confidence even of aged Christians, but rather a reason to treat him with affection. Gill widens the word: to neglect to take care of him would itself be to despise him, since he was employed in the same honourable work as the apostle — from which Gill infers that ministers' lives ought to be defended and secured by those to whom they minister, and their persons treated with esteem. Calvin suspects that this is exactly Paul's point, that failure to be concerned for Timothy's safety would already count as contempt, and he adds a third sense: they should not undervalue him out of ignorance of his worth. Clarke reads the charge as one about credentials — let none pretend to say that he has not full authority from God to do the work of an evangelist.

On the closing clauses Clarke breaks from the others twice. Following Bishop Pearce he would repunctuate, so that the sense is accompany him upon his journey, that he may come to me in peace, taking the word in its common sense of safety rather than as a description of the sending; Calvin independently glosses the same word as safety. Then Clarke denies the usual reading of the last clause altogether. It should not be understood as though Paul expected certain brethren to arrive with Timothy — it is the brethren already with Paul who are doing the looking, so that the sense is I, with the brethren, am looking for him. Wesley reads it the other way in four words, taking the brethren to be those accompanying Timothy, and Barnes agrees, naming Erastus as his companion and citing Grotius for the suggestion that Paul had asked Titus to bring some Corinthian brethren with him to Ephesus, where he might need their help.

Ellicott sets the arrangement in its sequence. Timothy and Erastus had been sent before this letter was written, at a time when the full state of affairs at Corinth had not yet reached the apostle; now that he knows how bad the case is and what vigorous treatment it needs, he sends the letter and with it Titus and two other brethren. Titus, Ellicott observes, was in energy and firmness of character a striking contrast to Timothy while equally sharing Paul's spirit and confidence, and so was competent and willing to deal with the recalcitrant temper of some parts of that church; the hope expressed here is that Timothy may join Titus and his party when they leave. Robertson supplies the sober outcome. Timothy did later have to return to Ephesus without much success, and was then sent on into Macedonia with Erastus, while Titus went to Corinth — the man Paul afterwards arranged to meet at Troas.
12:
Gill explains why the verse is needed at all. Apollos was a senior man to Timothy, an eloquent preacher who had worked at Corinth, was well known there and greatly approved by many; so the apostle takes trouble to excuse having sent the one and not the other, and to show that it was no fault of his. Calvin sets out the suspicion being headed off. Apollos had succeeded Paul in building up that church, and the better they knew him the more favourably they were disposed toward him and the readier they would be to conjecture that things had been deliberately contrived so that he should not come, out of some offence taken. They might well ask among themselves why these men had been sent to them rather than Apollos, and Paul's answer is that it was not owing to him. Barnes adds the likely occasion: the Corinthians had probably requested by the messengers who carried their letter that either Paul or Apollos would visit them, and Paul replies that he tried and did not succeed.

On why Apollos would not go, the bench is unanimous, which is itself worth noting. Clarke states it plainly: a faction had been set up in Apollos's name at Corinth, and he probably thought it imprudent to go just then lest his presence give that party either strength or countenance. Wesley suspects the same, that his coming might increase the divisions. Barnes reasons that he had perhaps left Corinth on account of the dissensions in the first place and would not return while they lasted, especially as the partisans had probably tried to make him the head of a party; and Barnes reports from the Latin fathers that Apollos did return there later, once the differences had been settled. Robertson is the bluntest — Apollos had left Corinth in disgust over the strife that involved both him and Paul, and had had enough of partisan quarrelling over preachers.

Ellicott draws out what the exchange shows about both men. Paul, free from the smallest spark of personal jealousy, had wished that Apollos — the very man whose name was being used as the banner of a faction against him — should be the one to carry this letter to Corinth; Paul had planted that church and Apollos had watered it, and in the planter's absence Apollos would have been the most likely and proper person to exercise authority there. That unselfishness, Ellicott says, is equalled by the thoughtful reluctance of Apollos, who feared his presence might encourage the one party and perhaps embitter the other, and so declined on the ground that it was not a convenient time. Ellicott will not let that word pass in its ordinary sense: in the thought of these teachers, convenient meant the good of Christ's church and not the ease or comfort of any individual man. Barnes takes the promise of a later visit as evidence that Apollos retained his affection and a tender solicitude for their peace, since without it they might have concluded he was offended and had no wish to come at all.
13:
Barnes takes the first imperative to mean keep awake, and suggests the figure may be drawn from the duty of a sentinel set to guard a camp and observe the enemy's movements: they are to watch as a sentinel watches, lest an enemy come suddenly upon a camp locked in sleep. Robertson confirms both verbs — the first means simply stay awake, and the later one, in the middle voice, means play the man. Gill first rules out a wrong object: they are not to watch for the coming of Apollos and a convenient season, but over themselves — their hearts, affections, words and whole conversation — and over one another, and against sin in its first motions, and against Satan, an indefatigable enemy whose wiles are many and cunning, and against false teachers lying in wait to deceive, of whom that church had many. Clarke gives the duty five directions at once: watch against evil, watch for opportunities to receive and to do good, watch over each other in love, and watch that none draw you aside from the belief and unity of the gospel.

Clarke then makes the observation that governs the verse — the terms in it are all military — and reads it straight through as a field order. Watch: keep your scouts out and your sentinels at their posts, lest your enemies steal a march on you. Stand fast: keep in your ranks, keep close together, for on your unity your preservation depends, and if the enemy succeeds in breaking your ranks and dividing one part of this sacred army from another your rout is inevitable. Quit yourselves like men: when attacked do not flinch, maintain your ground, resist, press forward, strike home, keep compact, conquer. Be strong: where one division is opposed by too great a force, strengthen it and hold the position, sustain each other, and do not fear, for fear will enervate you — your cause is good, Christ is your Captain in the field, and should you even die in the contest the victory is yours. Calvin sees the same campaign in it: because the warfare is incessant the watch must be incessant too, and he defines watchfulness of spirit as meditating on the things of God while free and disentangled from earthly cares, since the cares and lusts of the world, with idleness and carelessness, are a kind of spiritual drunkenness that leaves the mind drowsy and stupid.

Henry reads standing fast as a double command — to stand for the faith of the gospel and maintain it even to death, and to stand in it, abiding in its profession and yielding to its influence — and warns them not to surrender God's revelation for the world's wisdom. It is by faith alone, he adds, that a man keeps his ground in an hour of temptation, and by it that we overcome the world both when it fawns and when it frowns, when it tempts and when it terrifies; so the manly part is to behave strenuously against those who would split them into factions or seduce them from the faith, being neither terrified nor inveigled. Barnes notes that the verb for playing the man appears nowhere else in the New Testament, though it is frequent in the Greek Old Testament — in the charge to Joshua and in David's word to Solomon — and common in the classical writers; it means simply to show oneself a man and not a coward. Calvin observes that since we are naturally weak we must be told to gather strength, not assumed to have it. Wesley reduces the four commands to a line apiece: watch against all your enemies seen and unseen, stand fast by seeing and trusting him who is invisible, acquit yourselves with courage and patience, and be strong to do and to suffer all his will.
14:
Barnes glosses the opening phrase as simply all that you do, and notes that the direction is a repetition, explaining why the apostle risks one. It is given again because of its great importance, and because it sums up everything he has said in the letter — the long treatment of love a chapter or two earlier, and the ordering of the assembly that followed it, both come to rest here. Charity, Barnes says, was to regulate all that they did; it is a simple rule, and if it were observed everything would be done well. Calvin sees the same summary function, calling it the rule for all those transactions in which we have dealings with one another, and wishing love to be their directress in each of them. He then names the disease it answers: the Corinthians erred chiefly in this, that every one looked to himself without caring for others.

Gill spreads the word all across the three relations it must cover. Their whole obedience to Christ — their observation of and subjection to all his ordinances and commands — should spring from and be done in love to him. Their whole conduct toward one another should be governed by a charity which bears all things and covers a multitude of sins. And their church affairs, the business transacted at their meetings, should be handled not with strife and vainglory but in peace and mutual affection, with a concern for the good of each other and of the whole body, and for the glory of God.

The reason all three witnesses press the point is the same, and they say so. Gill observes that without charity, and the exercise of that grace, it signifies little what men either have or do — and that such an exhortation was the more necessary to this church precisely because it was so full of factions, contentions and divisions. Calvin's diagnosis of self-regard and Barnes's insistence that the rule is simple both point the same way: the trouble at Corinth was not that the church lacked gifts or knowledge, of which it had a great deal, but that it lacked the one thing that would have made either of them useful. So the shortest sentence in the chapter turns out to carry the weight of the whole epistle.
15:
Barnes warns that the construction is involved though the sense is plain: the entreaty begun here does not complete itself until the next verse, so that what stands between is a parenthesis giving the reasons why this household should be deferred to. Gill reads it the same way, that the whole account of Stephanas is set down as an argument for the submission afterwards required. What the household had done is described by a verb that carries the argument. Ellicott points to a play upon words in the Greek which can scarcely be rendered in English — they have ordered themselves to the ministry of the saints, and the Corinthians are now exhorted to order themselves under them in turn — so that the same root governs both halves of the appeal. Robertson lands on the same verb and calls the statement remarkable and worthy of attention still: this noble family appointed themselves to be ministers to the saints who needed it, nobody having appointed them. Personal work for Christ, he adds, is still the only way to win the world for Christ, voluntary personal work — if all Christians did it. Barnes fills in the shape that service took: aiding the ministry, showing hospitality, providing for the wants of others, attending and helping the apostles on their journeys.

On the title firstfruits the witnesses agree on the fact and differ on the weight. Wesley glosses it flatly as the first converts in that province, and Barnes notes that Paul had baptised this family himself and that a considerable part of it, perhaps all, had come to the faith. Clarke gives them a larger place, calling them the chief instruments of supporting the work of God in Achaia, of which work they had themselves been the firstfruits. Calvin is careful not to let priority alone confer rank: it is not that the first in order of time are in every case superior to the rest, but that where perseverance accompanies priority, honour is rightly given to those who have in a manner paved the way for the gospel by promptitude of faith. And he notes what actually earns the honourable title here — these were people who had consecrated their services and their resources to believers.

Calvin then draws the general principle out at length, and it is the boldest claim in the verse. We know from daily experience how much it matters that those whom God has adorned with the most distinguished gifts should hold the highest authority; so if we would secure the welfare of the church, let honour be conferred upon the good, let their counsels carry the greatest weight, and let others give way to them and allow themselves to be governed by their prudence. God manifests himself to us in showing us the gifts of his Spirit, and therefore, unless we would appear to despise God, we should yield willingly to those on whom he has conferred superior gifts. Ellicott turns the same coin over: the devotion of teachers and of all who serve in the ministry ought to be repaid with a return of sympathy and devotion from those they serve. He adds the delicate circumstance behind the commendation. Stephanas and his companions had come to Ephesus, probably carrying the Corinthians' own letter, and being faithful amid the faithless had made up for the want of zeal in so many; but the Corinthians might well suspect them of having carried tales about the state of their church, and so Paul commends them expressly as friends who came on behalf of the whole body, not as accusers.
16:
How far the submission reaches is the one real question here, and the bench divides. Clarke states the narrow view flatly: the submission recommended does not imply obedience, but a kind and courteous demeanour — due regard for such men, considering them as special instruments in God's hand for carrying on his work — and he cites Kypke as vindicating that sense of the word from its use elsewhere of Christians yielding to one another and of the younger to the elder. Barnes takes it much the same way, that the word evidently means to show proper deference and regard, treating such people with distinguished respect and honour for what they have done. Gill reaches considerably further. He divides the duty according to the kind of service rendered: where men minister to poor saints, submission means assisting them and putting it in their power to discharge that work fully; where men labour in the ministry of the word, it means attending their ministrations, receiving the truths they deliver with faith and love, hearkening to their admonitions and counsel, regarding the censures and reproofs they pass by the authority of the church and in its name, and living in subjection to the laws of Christ's house as those men administer them.

Gill does not leave that unqualified, and the qualification is the interesting part. The truths delivered are to be received with faith and love only so far as they appear to be agreeable to the word of God — which sets a limit inside the very duty he has just drawn so widely, and keeps the deference from becoming unconditional. Between Clarke's courteous demeanour and Gill's regarded censures there is a real distance, and the verse itself does not settle it; what both agree on is that the honour is owed for work actually done and not for office merely held.

The others read the verse as completing the sentence begun before it. Robertson says plainly that this is the exhortation started in the previous verse — the family of Stephanas took the lead in good works, and the Corinthians are to follow such leaders — and then turns it on his own readers: this is our great problem still, to find great leaders and many loyal followers, and that would solve all church problems; lend a hand. Wesley catches the reciprocity in three words, that the Corinthians are to submit in their turn, so repaying the free service they had received. Both Wesley and Barnes note that the charge does not stop with Stephanas. Wesley extends it to everyone who labours in the gospel, whether with a fellow-labourer or without one; Barnes suggests that since Corinth was a central place and a thoroughfare, others who were Paul's personal friends and had aided him in the ministry would be passing among them, and that his request covers all such.
17:
Clarke identifies the errand at once: it was by these three that the Corinthians had sent the letter which this epistle was largely written to answer. Barnes supposes Stephanas was chosen for it as one of the oldest and most respected members of that church, sent both to carry the letter and to consult with the apostle about their affairs. Gill thinks they were very probably of the household of Chloe, and observes that whether they came of their own accord or as the church's messengers, one of them had been baptised by Paul and perhaps all were converted under his ministry — believers certainly, and quite possibly ministers of the gospel. Of the other two, Barnes notes that they are named nowhere else in the New Testament; but both he and Clarke report that Fortunatus outlived Paul, and appears afterwards as the messenger who carried Clement's letter from Rome back to the Corinthians. Robertson pauses on the word for their coming: it is the very term used of the coming of Christ, here spent on the arrival of three men from Corinth.

What exactly they made up is the crux, and nobody can settle it. Barnes explains that the noun rendered that which was lacking does not occur in the classical writers at all and means simply a want or deficiency, which may be a want of support, of sustenance, of aid, of consolation, of information or of counsel — so that what the Corinthians had failed to furnish can only be conjectured. He offers three possibilities: that they had neglected to provide for Paul's material wants; that their letter had been defective in telling him about their affairs; or that these men had supplied by their presence and conversation the friendly offices the whole church would have rendered had it been there.

Clarke narrows the field to two of those, either additional communications beyond what the letter contained — from which Paul had a fuller account of their spiritual state than the letter gave — or some contribution toward the apostle's support in his travels and labours. Robertson refuses to choose at all, and for a reason of grammar rather than of history: the phrase can mean either that these men filled up his lack of the Corinthians or that they filled up their lack of him. Either makes perfectly good sense, both were true, and which Paul meant we cannot tell. Wesley quietly adopts the second, saying that they performed the offices of love which the Corinthians could not perform themselves by reason of their absence; and he notes that by the time this was written the three had already gone home again, though the joy their arrival caused remained still in the apostle's heart.
18:
Gill explains what the refreshment consisted in. The very sight of the three gave the apostle joy, their Christian discourse more, and most of all the account they brought of the church itself. Much in that account was disagreeable and is the occasion of this letter; but much was pleasing, and Gill thinks Paul's spirit had been greatly depressed by reports reaching him from another quarter, and by the fear that matters stood worse than they really did. From these brethren he learned that many in the church had great grace and large gifts and came behind none in such things, that they stood steadfast in the faith of the gospel and opposed the false teachers vigorously, and that they sought in everything the welfare of the church and the interest of Christ. Robertson notes that the verb chosen for this refreshing is the very one Jesus used of the rest he offers to those who come to him — fellowship with Christ there, and here fellowship of Christians with each other.

The clause and yours is read four different ways, and Barnes lays the options side by side. Locke takes it to mean that the visit refreshed both parties by removing the suspicions and fears that stood on either side. Bloomfield holds that by supplying the absence of the Corinthians these men benefited both, since Paul gained information about those who were away while they gained the counsel the apostle could give them. Doddridge reads it of their conduct at home, that as they had refreshed Paul by their obliging behaviour and edifying conversation, so no doubt they had often refreshed the Corinthians by their ministrations among them. Clarke takes the simplest line, that what contributed greatly to his comfort must for that reason increase theirs, and Wesley says the same in five words — inasmuch as you share in my comfort. Barnes's own judgement gathers the rest: the visit would benefit both sides, imparting comfort and a good understanding and an increase of mutual attachment, and in the end a large accession to their joy when they should meet again.

On the charge that follows, Barnes takes acknowledge to mean receive them affectionately, recognise them as brethren and cherish them, and specifically that the Corinthians should welcome these three on their return and regard with deference the counsel they might offer and the message they carried. Wesley asks for suitable love and respect. Clarke turns the instruction into a general rule of the sharpest kind, and it answers the party spirit this whole letter has been fighting: let all be held in esteem in proportion to their work and usefulness. When that is made the measure of respect, he says, foolish and capricious attachments will have no place at all; a man will be honoured in proportion to his merit, and his merit will be estimated by his usefulness among men.
19:
Barnes explains that Asia in the New Testament usually means Asia Minor at large but is sometimes narrowed to the country around Ephesus, of which that city was the centre and capital, and it is undoubtedly the narrower sense here; Robertson agrees that the phrase is true of the Roman province, and remarks how rapidly the gospel had spread out from Ephesus. Gill notes that the Syriac makes it all the churches. Then all three of the older witnesses turn the greeting into evidence about the letter's origin, for a third time in this chapter. Gill argues that from Philippi he would have sent greetings from the churches of Macedonia rather than of Asia, and Clarke makes the identical point. Calvin adds the corroboration from the couple named next, since Luke tells us that Aquila and Priscilla stayed on at Ephesus when Paul went elsewhere. Barnes glosses the warmth of the greeting itself — much in the Lord means as Christians, with affectionate Christian salutation, wishing one another the blessing and favour of the Lord.

What the church in their house was is genuinely disputed. Calvin calls the phrase a magnificent eulogium, since the name of the Church is here applied to a single family, and holds that all the families of the pious ought to be so ordered as to be so many little churches; he rejects the alternative word Erasmus preferred as foreign to Paul's design, since the apostle did not mean to designate a crowd by a common term but to speak honourably of the management of a Christian household. Henry takes the same view, that the family itself is very probably what is called the church in their house, and draws the consequence out: every Christian family should in some respects be a Christian church — cast away on a foreign shore with no other believers they should be a church themselves, if large enough, and use all the ordinances, while in ordinary cases they should live under Christian rules and daily offer up Christian worship, for wherever two or three are gathered and Christ is among them there is a church. Clarke reads it of the congregation instead, pointing out that there were no churches or chapels built at that time, so that assemblies were necessarily held in private houses; Aquila and Priscilla devoted theirs to the purpose, as Philemon and Nymphas did after them. Ellicott offers a third and narrower possibility, that the phrase means a group of foreigners then resident in Ephesus who met there for worship, as distinct from those who had been converted in the city.

Robertson adds the circumstance that makes Clarke's reading concrete. Paul had long since left the synagogue for the lecture hall of Tyrannus, but Aquila and Prisca opened their own house for the services, and the churches had to meet where they could. He also notes that this was their habit wherever they lived, and that Paul had laboured and lodged with this family first at Corinth and now again at Ephesus; Wesley records the same beginning, that the apostle's acquaintance with them started during their stay at Corinth, and Ellicott that they had been his friends there. Henry pauses over the fact that such greetings are in the letter at all, and makes it a point of principle. Christianity does by no means destroy civility and good manners, and Paul could find room in an epistle treating of very weighty matters to pass on the good wishes of friends; those misrepresent religion who take any encouragement from it to be sour and morose. Nor are such salutations empty compliments — they carry real expressions of goodwill, and those who salute in the Lord wish their brethren all good from the Lord and breathe out their wishes in fervent prayer.
20:
Gill offers three candidates for the brethren who send this greeting: the members of the church at Ephesus, or Paul's fellow-workers in the ministry who were with him, Sosthenes and the rest, or the three men lately arrived from Corinth. Barnes takes it simply of all the Christians with whom Paul was connected at Ephesus, and notes that they felt a deep interest in the Corinthian church. On the manner of greeting Clarke explains the background: the ancient patriarchs and the Jews generally were accustomed to kiss one another whenever they met, this being with them a token of friendship and peace much as the shaking of hands is with us, and the primitive Christians naturally followed the example. Ellicott says the same of the wider East, where the kiss was the ordinary form of affectionate greeting; the Church took it over, and when it passed between people whose bond of friendship was not earthly but spiritual it came to be called the holy kiss.

Calvin thinks the reference here is not to greeting in general but to a solemn kiss with which they saluted one another in the sacred assembly, and says he could easily believe that from the times of the apostles it was used in connection with the administration of the Supper. His text carries a long note gathering the evidence for that. Justin Martyr, writing in the earlier part of the second century, describes the Christians' customs thus: after the prayers, we embrace each other with a kiss. Tertullian speaks of it as an ordinary part of the services of the Lord's day. Origen says that from this very precept the custom was handed down to the churches, that after prayer the brethren should salute one another so. The Apostolical Constitutions describe the manner: let the men apart, and the women apart, salute each other with a kiss in the Lord — which independently confirms what Robertson observes, that in the synagogue men kissed men and women kissed women, and that the practice seems never to have been promiscuous between the sexes. Ellicott traces its end, noting that the Latin Church gave it up in the thirteenth century while the Greek Church keeps it still on certain great occasions such as Easter Day.

What the kiss meant is stated most fully by Cyril of Jerusalem, who describes the moment in the liturgy when the deacon cries aloud, receive ye one another, and let us kiss one another. Do not think, he warns, that this kiss is of the same character as those given in public by common friends; it is not such. This kiss blends souls one with another and courts entire forgiveness for them; it is the sign that our souls are mingled together and have banished all remembrance of wrongs. Cyril grounds it in the Lord's own command that a man who remembers at the altar that his brother has something against him should leave his gift, go and be reconciled first, and then come and offer — and so concludes that the kiss is reconciliation, and that this is why it is holy, citing both Paul's holy kiss here and Peter's kiss of charity. Cyril's account is a fourth-century confirmation of exactly what Calvin had guessed at. The note in Calvin's text is nevertheless cautious about pressing the precept further: that Paul meant the Corinthians to salute one another on receiving this letter is certain, but that he meant to make it an everlasting ordinance in all churches has never been proved and is by no means likely. It adds a melancholy postscript — the very prevalence of the custom probably gave rise to the calumny that Christians indulged in licentiousness at their meetings, and the wish to leave calumniators no occasion is likely what brought the practice to an end.
21:
All six witnesses agree on the fact behind the verse: the letter was dictated, and this line marks the point where the apostle takes the pen himself. Wesley says it in seven words, that what precedes was written by an amanuensis. Clarke would make the grammar show it, arguing that the clause should be rendered the salutation is written by the hand of me Paul, with the verb understood, and thinks it very likely that Paul wrote this verse and those following in his own hand while the rest, though dictated by him, was written out by another. Robertson gives the literal sense as with the hand of me Paul, explains the odd apposition of the genitive with the possessive pronoun, and observes that this is the sign in every epistle: he dictated, but signed at the end. Then Robertson allows himself a wish that most readers will share — if we only had that signature on that scrap of paper.

Why the signature mattered is put most fully by Gill and Barnes, and they agree. Gill says the apostle wrote his common salutation in his own hand to prevent counterfeits, so that the church he wrote to might be assured the letter was genuinely his. Barnes lists what the practice accomplished: it gave a sanction to what was written, proved the letter to be his own, served as a valuable token of affectionate regard, and was evidence that there was no fraud or imposition in the case. Both note that Paul made a settled habit of it, signing his name and adding his Christian salutation in every letter.

On who actually held the pen for the rest, Barnes is candid that he does not know — why Paul employed an amanuensis at all, he says, is not known. Ellicott is willing to name one. It was the apostle's habit to dictate his letters but to add a few words at the close in his own writing, so that the concluding verses here are his autograph; and the earlier portions of this letter, Ellicott suggests, had been written by Sosthenes, whose name stands beside Paul's in the opening greeting. Whether that identification holds or not, the effect the witnesses describe is the same: a letter that arrives with a handwritten close carries its own proof of authorship, and a church torn by rival claims to apostolic authority would have needed it.
22:
Barnes calls this a most solemn and affecting close, aimed at everything the letter has been fighting. It turns their minds from the disputes that had rent the church into factions and puts one question in their place: do they love the Saviour? The danger, Barnes says, was that in their strife over minor matters they should substitute attachment to a party for the love of Christ. Ellicott adds that with his own hand the apostle brings them back from all the argument of the epistle to the true test of their Christianity, and that the word for love signifies not merely affectionate regard but personal devotion. Calvin identifies the offenders sharply: not strangers who avowedly hated the Christian name, but pretenders and hypocrites who troubled the churches for the sake of their own belly or from empty boasting. He traces the disorder to its root, since a sincere love to Christ will not suffer us to give occasion of offence to the brethren. Robertson agrees that it is the nominal Christian's refusal to love Christ that deserves the word.

Gill canvasses the alternatives and rules one out. The apostle does not mean profane sinners who lack love to Christ through ignorance, nor even those who from that ignorance persecute him in his members, for such are to be prayed for and are often called by grace afterwards, as Gill notes the apostle himself was. Clarke has no doubt: the sentence is directed against the Jews, who had called Jesus accursed, and Paul now retorts it upon them. Clarke also describes the three Jewish forms of the sentence — the niddui, a thirty-day exclusion from synagogue, wife and family; the cherem, laid with dire execrations on a man who had not made compensation within those days, though it always left room for repentance; and the shammatha, direst of all, which cut off every hope of reconciliation. Yet Clarke insists the apostle is not wishing or imprecating but predicting what would certainly come without repentance, and Barnes agrees that the words express a truth about God's dealings rather than any desire of Paul's. Calvin doubts whether Paul seeks their destruction before God or means to render them execrable in the eyes of believers; recalling his reading of a similar curse elsewhere as let him be held by you as accursed, he settles for a plain sense: let them perish and be cut off, as being the pests of the church.

The last word divides the ancient readers from the modern ones. Wesley reports the older understanding, that the Jews of that age, having pronounced a man anathema, customarily added the Syriac Maran-atha, the Lord cometh — namely, to execute vengeance upon him; and Barnes explains why the addition mattered: though no earthly power could punish a want of love to Christ, no one could escape, because the Lord would come himself. Ellicott and Robertson both deny that the two words belong together. Ellicott would print them as separate sentences, and takes the second to mean the Lord is at hand rather than the Lord is come, the uncertainty of the moment being the most solemn thought with which to press the importance of being one with Christ. Robertson calls it a curious blunder in the King James Version that the phrase was ever joined to the curse, reading it instead as a watchword expressing the lively hope of Christ's coming. Calvin reports that almost all the ancients agree the terms are Syriac, and objects to one proposed rendering as supposing absurdly that the apostle would address Greeks in Syriac — his text being damaged where his own conclusion should stand. Wesley adds that Paul chose to write this weighty sentence in his own hand and to set it between the salutation and the benediction, so that it might be the more attentively regarded.
23:
Gill begins with the formula rather than its content, noting that this is the apostle's salutation in all his epistles and that its presence is itself a token of their truth and genuineness — a signature of authorship, not merely a closing courtesy, and the natural sequel to the verse in which Paul took the pen into his own hand. What it asks for, on Gill's reading, has two parts that are easily run together. It is first a wish for a supply of all grace from Christ, and then, distinctly, a wish for the increase of that grace in the saints — a benediction pronounced over people who already possess the thing prayed for, asking only that they receive more of it. Gill's word is supply, which implies a continuing provision rather than a single gift.

Gill then unfolds what such communications of grace actually do, and he names four effects in order. They quicken, which is to say they bring to life what was dormant; they invigorate, adding strength to what is already alive; they draw forth into exercise the grace the saints have already received, so that what was held becomes what is used; and they enable and assist in the discharge of every duty. The sequence matters, since on this account grace is not only what saves a man at the outset but what continues to move him afterwards, and the benediction is therefore addressed to the whole of the Christian life rather than to its beginning.

Clarke's paraphrase widens the single word grace into four, asking that the favour, the influence, the mercy and the salvation procured by Jesus Christ may all be with them. He then turns the prayer through three prepositions, each marking a further degree of possession: that this grace may prevail among them, which is a matter of the church's common life; that it may rule in them, which reaches the individual will; and that it may be exhibited by them, in their life and conversation, which carries it back out into view. Set against everything the letter has recorded of this church — its factions, its lawsuits, its disorders at the table — the progression reads as a summary of precisely what had been missing, and Clarke closes it, as the apostle does, with an Amen.
24:
Ellicott catches the effect of the ending in a single image: like a river which, after rushing and foaming over many a rock and through many a gorge, at last emerges into a broad calm amid sunlit meadows, so this epistle, after chapters of trenchant logic and fervid rebuke, closes in peaceful words of tenderness and love. Barnes locates the force of that contrast precisely: the close is peculiarly tender when we remember how many of these people had treated Paul, and that it follows immediately upon the solemn curse of the previous verse. Gill offers two ways of taking the words. Either the apostle desires to be loved as he loves them, keeping a place in their affections as they had in his; or he commends to them a love of his own reaching all without exception, rich and poor, greater and lesser believers alike. And it is to forestall any suspicion that this was a merely natural fondness, or built on outward advantages, that Paul adds the last three words — which Barnes glosses as meaning through Christ, or in connection with their own love to him, that is, as Christians.

Clarke will not let the sentence stand as it reads, and his objection is worth stating in full because it is a question of sense before it is one of manuscripts. We can easily conceive what the grace of Christ be with you means, he says: grace is an active, powerful, saving principle, essential to the very existence of the church, and without it no individual can be saved. But what could the apostle's love do with them? He confesses he can see no meaning in it, unless it amounts to saying no more than I love you, or I continue to love you. He then finds textual support for his unease: the possessive pronoun is absent from the Codex Alexandrinus and from an excellent eleventh-century Vatican manuscript, which yields either may love prevail among you or, if one supplies the word for God as Paul does at the end of the second epistle to this same church, the love of God be with you. That, Clarke argues, gives a sound sense, since the love of God is as much a principle of light and life and salvation as the grace of Christ; and he suspects the pronoun is simply a copyist's corruption of the divine name. He adds that the closing Amen is wanting in most manuscripts of repute and was certainly not written by the apostle.

Both Barnes and Clarke then turn on the note appended after the last verse in the common editions, and neither is gentle. Clarke calls it palpably absurd: it cannot have been written from Philippi, and it could not have been carried by the four men it names. He lists the rival forms to show how little any of them is worth — some say only that the first letter to the Corinthians is finished, others give Ephesus, or Asia, or Philippi of Macedonia; the Syriac adds that it was sent by the hand of Timothy, the Coptic by Stephanas and Fortunatus, while another makes Paul and Sosthenes the writers. Barnes states the principle behind the objection. The subscription was plainly written by some hand other than Paul's and has no claim whatever to be regarded as inspired; such notes were probably added long after the letters themselves, in some cases by people not well informed. In this instance, he says flatly, the subscription is in its main statement false, and it is absurd to suppose Timothy carried the letter when the letter itself shows him already away among the churches. None of the manuscript forms carries any authority, and since such subscriptions generally mislead the reader of the Bible, Barnes judges it would have been better had they been omitted altogether.
